title: Moderna shares plunge after cancer vaccine data leaks — despite positive results
description: Timon Schneider | SOPA Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesModerna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its
body: Timon Schneider | SOPA Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesModerna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its closely watched cancer vaccine developed with Merck. Shares of both drugmakers fell even though the data, released in full later Thursday following the leak, appeared meaningful for patients and positive relative to Wall Street expectations. The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone. The data also showed that the shot along with Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy. The companies said about 82% of patients who received the personalized cancer vaccine alongside Keytruda were alive without their melanoma returning at two years after receiving the shot, compared with 70% of those who received Keytruda alone."This is a huge development for our patients," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD ​Anderson Cancer Center, about the results. He said that the added benefit of the vaccine also comes with much milder toxicity, or side effects like injection-site pain, compared to other cancer treatments. The detailed phase 3 trial results were set to be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference this weekend. "Whenever you put a therapy on top of something that works really well, like Keytruda, sometimes it's harder to show additional benefit. We have no problems of showing additional benefit here," Dr. Dean Li, Merck Research Laboratories president, said in an interview ahead of the results. The benefit appeared even larger after the six-month vaccine regimen, with a separate analysis showing a 58% reduction in risk of recurrence or death. The companies say it is still too early to determine whether the treatment helps patients live longer overall.Several analysts acknowledged investors' elevated expectations ahead of the release, but noted that the data is overall positive."We assert this relative reduction in recurrence/death is clinically meaningful," BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman said in a research note on Thursday following the leak. "Such a [stock] reaction likely reflects inflated expectations into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy."Oncologists and investors see the targeted vaccine as a possible breakthrough treatment, with the potential to be used to treat other forms of cancer in the future. Merck and Moderna are studying the vaccine in several trials across other tumors, such as non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma. But Li acknowledged the companies have more work to show the product can be effective across tumor types. "I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Li said. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."The shot is designed to target the specific mutations in each patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach. The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Keytruda, which helps the body attack the cancer more effectively.It could also offer Moderna a critical additional commercial product in its pipeline, following vaccines for Covid-19, the flu and respiratory syncytial virus.In a research note Thursday, UBS analysts said "this is overall a strong data set" and gives more confidence in upcoming studies of the vaccine in kidney and bladder cancers. They added the stock reaction may be due more to massive expectations than disappointing data. Against the backdrop of those high expectations, Moderna shares have spiked more than 530% year-to-date as of Thursday afternoon. Shares of Merck, a much larger drugmaker, fell by about 1% on Thursday. The company's stock has climbed nearly 41% this year.Since the vaccine is personalized, the complicated manufacturing process can take six weeks. But Merck CEO Robert Davis told CNBC last week that the company believes it can shorten that timeline in the future, potentially allowing the shot to reach more patients more quickly.

schema.headline: Moderna shares plunge after cancer vaccine data leaks — despite positive results

title: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform
description: Adamdodd | GettyAmerican Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform. The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring m
body: Adamdodd | GettyAmerican Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform. The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs. Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking. "We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release. Membership points vary by card: Consumer and Business Platinum Card members earn five times the membership rewards on prepaid Airbnb bookings through Amex Travel. Consumer Classic Green Card members earn three times the points on travel bookings made directly through third-party sites, including Airbnb. Other eligible rewards members earn two times the points on prepaid Airbnb bookings through Amex Travel.The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up. Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers. Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges, with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to their travel plans this summer, a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

schema.headline: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform

title: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.
description: A staff member is seen at a Taco Bell restaurant in London.May James | Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesPepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their lon
body: A staff member is seen at a Taco Bell restaurant in London.May James | Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesPepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036, the food and beverage company said Thursday.The announcement comes one week after Taco Bell's sister chain, KFC, said that it will switch to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. While it is unusual for large restaurant chains to change drink providers, the move is not unprecedented, as Coke and Pepsi try to win contracts through perks and other inducements. Coke's win over Pepsi was more symbolic, representing another example of how the Atlanta-based company has been beating its rival in the soda category.Pepsi's relationship with Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands spans decades, back to when the beverage giant owned the restaurant chains before spinning them into a separate public company in 1997. Despite KFC's defection in the U.S., Pepsi remains an important partner for Yum and the chain's international markets, KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo on Oct. 15 that was obtained by CNBC. Thanks to its partnership with Pepsi, Taco Bell has long served exclusive menu items that use Pepsi products, like Mountain Dew Baja Blast and Doritos Locos Tacos, at its restaurants.The renewed deal also means that Taco Bell international markets such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand will serve Pepsi products.

schema.headline: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.

title: Trump asked Musk to lift Starlink slowdown, WSJ reports
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump asked Elon Musk to ease restrictions he had imposed on the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink system in Ukrai
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump asked Elon Musk to ease restrictions he had imposed on the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink system in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials.The Starshield system, which Ukraine depends on in its war against Russia, was "working more normally Thursday, shortly after" Trump spoke to Musk by phone, U.S. and Ukrainian officials told the Journal.Trump said later Thursday he did not "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk."Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference," Trump told reporters outside the White House as he departed for a campaign rally in Iowa."The bottom line, he put it back," Trump said of Musk.The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX and a critic of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, had ordered the Starlink slowdown. Two unnamed sources in that report said Trump and Musk had discussed the decision to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, while one source said Musk had spoken to Trump prior to imposing the speed cap.Trump has repeatedly denied involvement in the decision and said he does not know if Musk was behind it."I don't know who did it, but I was not involved," Trump said Wednesday.The Starlink controversy, which drew bipartisan concern and criticism from lawmakers, emerged as Trump has ramped up criticism of Zelenskyy for continuing to target Russian energy infrastructure. At the same time, Trump has pursued a deal to ease sanctions on Russia so it can supply some diesel on the global market.Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the ranking member of the Senate homeland security committee's investigations subcommittee, on Thursday launched an inquiry into how SpaceX's satellite tech was "degraded for Ukraine without notice.""This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally not only put Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril, but raises serious questions about who controls critical capabilities the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to procure," Blumenthal said in letters to Musk and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.The White House and an email associated with Musk did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Thursday's report that Trump had asked Musk to lift the restrictions.

schema.headline: Trump asked Musk to lift Starlink slowdown, WSJ reports

title: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 17, 2025.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesIn case t
body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 17, 2025.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesIn case there were any doubts, Mark Zuckerberg is staying in California.Meta was apparently concerned enough that its founder and CEO might depart its home state that the company put in place a new stock plan that could help offset the burden of higher taxes should a billionaires tax, known as Proposition 40, pass on Election Day on Nov. 3. The disclosure came in a filing on Wednesday that coincided with Meta's third-quarter earnings report, and represents a first among California's mega-cap tech companies. Zuckerberg, the sixth-richest person in the world, is one of the few among his peers to still reside in the state, along with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.Elon Musk and Michael Dell live in Texas, while Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' primary residence has always been elsewhere. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin moved out of California ahead of the election and bought luxury homes in Florida, the same state that Oracle founder Larry Ellison officially calls home. Prop. 40 would impose a 5% tax on Californians worth over $1 billion. Zuckerberg's net worth is currently about $225 billion. "If the California wealth tax is enacted and Mr. Zuckerberg becomes liable for a tax payment, Mr. Zuckerberg would effectively be paying to serve as the Company's chief executive officer while residing in California," the filing said, noting the CEO's "salary of only $1 each year."Meta said in the filing that Zuckerberg committed to remaining in California for eight years, "unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."The company created a new class of non-voting Class C common stock to take effect in January. Zuckerberg will essentially be granted a portion of the new stock via a dividend. He will be able to "immediately sell or transfer up to 20%" of the shares he's granted "for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control," the filing said."There were many driving factors that led the board and special committee to approve the Class C shares, and it would be misleading to attribute it to any single reason," Meta told CNBC in a statement.The tech industry, by and large, has been unified in its objection to the ballot measure. In addition to the Google co-founders, a number of big-name techies have put spending into opposing Prop. 40. They include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, venture investor Peter Thiel and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, according to various media reports based on campaign filings.Collison and Xu are members of Meta's board of directors while Thiel left the company's board in 2022, having served since 2005.Brin told The New York Times in April he fled the Soviet Union with his family in 1979, and said, "I don't want California to end up in the same place."Huang, however, recently told CBS Sunday Morning that it would be a "privilege" to pay the tax. Huang is just behind Zuckerberg in Forbes' billionaire ranking, with a net worth of $185 billion.Although Prop. 40 advocates, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., have been urging voters to pass the ballot measure, recent polling has suggested that it may fail to garner the majority support required to make it law. A recent Citrin-Politico poll showed 46% are in favor of the measure compared with 43% who oppose it.Meta, with the help of a special committee, views Zuckerberg as key to the company's future and its efforts to become a major player in artificial intelligence, according to the filing. In particular, the company said it doesn't want to jeopardize Zuckerberg's close working arrangement with the Meta Superintelligence Labs, which is led by AI chief Alexandr Wang."The Special Committee believes that Mr. Zuckerberg's talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the Special Committee wants that to continue," the filing said.Although Meta considered the possibility of issuing Class A common stock to help raise funds, the filing noted that Zuckerberg made clear "that he would not support a significant equity financing that would have the effect of reducing his voting power in the Company."Instead, the new stock incentive will help Meta receive "critical equity capital without impacting Mr. Zuckerberg's voting power and the unique and creative vision and exceptional management abilities which helped to deliver the long-term value as noted above," the filing said.WATCH: 'Fast Money' traders react to Meta's Q3 results as stock climbs in extended trading.

schema.headline: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election

title: Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit by Dec. 11: Reports
description: US President Donald Trump during an executive order (EO) signing in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026
body: US President Donald Trump during an executive order (EO) signing in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. The executive order will establish a women's health office at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Photographer: Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesA federal judge in Miami on Thursday ordered that President Donald Trump sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11, according to multiple news outlets.U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, at a court hearing Thursday, also warned Trump's attorneys that if the president does not comply with court orders to give lawyers for the British media outlet records that are relevant to the lawsuit, his complaint could be dismissed, Politico reported.  Trump's lawyers had requested that his deposition be conducted between Jan. 11 and Jan. 22. Charles Tobin, the attorney for the BBC, told Lett at the hearing that although Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on Oct. 16, the president canceled it for a "matter of national importance," The Associated Press reported.But in fact, Tobin said, Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day, the AP reported."He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition," Tobin told judge.When contacted by CNBC for comment, the BBC said: "We have nothing to add."Lawyers for the BBC in a recent court filing had accused Trump's legal team of foot-dragging in complying with requests for documents and records relevant to the case, a process known as discovery."With just two months of discovery remaining, Plaintiff has not even tried to comply withhis discovery obligations," the filing said. "Neither production included documents that were even plausibly in Plaintiff's possession. Instead, Plaintiff has repeatedly sent back documents that the BBC already produced to him during discovery, and his counsel trawled the internet in the days before production to find publicly available webpages."Trump sued the BBC on Dec. 15, alleging that the outlet produced a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump" in a Panorama documentary aired one week before the 2024 presidential election.The suit alleges that the documentary was produced as part of a "brazen attempt" to interfere with and to influence the outcome of the election "to President Trump's detriment."The complaint claims that the documentary, "Trump: A Second Chance," was edited to make it falsely appear that during his Jan. 6, 2021, speech outside the White House, Trump explicitly urged his supporters to attack the U.S. Capitol.The BBC's chair apologized for the edit shortly before the suit was filed. The BBC also promised not to air the documentary again or show it on any of its platforms."While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip  was edited, we strongly disagree there is a basis for a defamation  claim," the broadcaster said in a statement on Nov. 13, 2025.— CNBC's Ryan Ruggiero contributed to this article.

schema.headline: Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit by Dec. 11: Reports

title: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
description: A job seeker holds paperwork during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on Sept. 25, 2026 in Sunrise, Florida. J
body: A job seeker holds paperwork during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on Sept. 25, 2026 in Sunrise, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesEmployers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29. Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period."Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6.Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates. Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.Correction: The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6. An earlier version misstated the month and date.

schema.headline: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues

title: AI debt and French bonds face a stress test — why it may not be over
description: A protester waving a French national flag walks past a fire during clashes prior to the start of a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of
body: A protester waving a French national flag walks past a fire during clashes prior to the start of a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", in Marseille, southern France, on Oct. 17, 2026.Thibaud Moritz | AFP | Getty ImagesFrom AI companies financing data center projects to France's heavily indebted government, credit markets are flashing warnings as investors grow warier of borrowing risks.Five-year credit default swap spreads have widened for CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank Group, as well as France and Italy, according to CNBC's analysis of FactSet data. AI-related bonds have been selling off as markets raise the cost of capital amid concerns of a financing crunch. Neocloud demand is "off the charts," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC on Thursday, but he warned of a "scarcity of capital." "The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," he said, adding, "that's going to get solved."Countries like France face a similar crunch. Pressure is building in bond markets as investors demand more compensation to finance public debt. Recent mass protests and rioting in France have heightened the market's concerns."Markets may no longer want to underwrite massive capex, heavy leverage, and uncertain future cash flows, and that same shift is widening French sovereign spreads as investors demand more compensation to hold long‑duration, debt‑financed obligations from a strained state,"  FedWatch Advisors CIO and founder Ben Emons wrote on his "French Neoclouds" Substack post. Insurance costs rise for AI-linked debtCoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are at the heart of the AI infrastructure buildout, spanning data centers, cloud services and financing.Their five-year CDS spreads offer a window into investors' anxiety about the cost of it all and eventual payoff. Higher spreads mean more expensive default protection and can signal greater concern about a borrower's creditworthiness.CoreWeave has experienced some of the sharpest increases in default-protection costs. Its five-year CDS spread reached 1,065.84 basis points on Oct. 21, according to FactSet, reflecting heightened concerns about the debt-heavy company's ability to finance its expansion.At the same time Oracle's spread rose to 308.25 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 141 on Jan. 2. S&P Credit Ratings downgraded Oracle's debt to the lowest level of investment grade in July, citing the expanding infrastructure business raised the overall credit risk. Softbank is a major AI investor with a large stake in OpenAI and investments in data centers and power infrastructure, including an $87 billion commitment for data centers in France. Its five-year CDS spread stood near a four-year high of 432 basis points on Oct. 20, up from 284 basis points on Jan. 5.  France's default-protection costs climb above Italy'sFrance isn't in a full-fledged debt crisis, but markets are signaling unease with the cost of protecting against a sovereign default rising above that of Italy's, which has also increased.France's five-year credit default swap spread reached 89.8 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 29.74 basis points on Jan. 2, according to CNBC's analysis. Italy's spread increased to 67.1 basis points on Oct. 22 from 28.33 on Jan 2. France's budget uncertainty and debt burden have become a focus, raising concerns that the risk could spill over to other countries in Europe.Germany's spread also rose but remained much lower at 12.15 basis points on Oct. 22, compared with 7.47 at the start of the period.Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group, pointed to France's mounting debt burden and persistent fiscal deficits as key drivers of rising default-protection costs."The key drivers are the large amount of French sovereign debt (120% of GDP) and the inability to reduce the deficit," Wizman told CNBC. In comparison to France, German government debt is 65% of the country's GDP.Investors are also watching the spread between French and German bonds, considered the European benchmark of creditworthiness, which has also surged to 1.6 percentage points. France's 10-year bond yield also topped 5% for the first time since 2002. The spread between the 10-year yield on French OATs and German Bunds is the extra payment investors demand to hold French bonds instead of German.While the Franco-German spread is relatively wide, the Eurozone saw far larger gaps in borrowing costs during the Eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s.France faces another test on Oct. 23 when Moody's is scheduled to review its Aa3 sovereign rating, which carries a negative outlook. The review comes as political divisions complicate efforts to repair the country's public finances.Spillover effects to bond indexes  While stresses are popping up in some pockets of AI financing, debt markets are also pricing in higher costs. S&P Global warned on Oct. 19 that major cloud providers may have more AI-linked debt exposure than publicly recognized.  CDS indexes offer a broader picture of credit-market pressure by tracking default-protection costs across baskets of companies.North America's CDX High Yield index captures credit risk across speculative-grade companies. Its five-year midpoint spread reached 355.35 basis points on Oct. 20, up about 39 basis points from the end of 2025, according to data from LSEG.The widening suggests investors are demanding more compensation for credit risk beyond AI-linked borrowers.

schema.headline: AI debt and French bonds face a stress test — why it may not be over

title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism
description: U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (L) during an election rally at the Covelli Centre on O
body: U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (L) during an election rally at the Covelli Centre on Oct. 12, 2026 in Youngstown, Ohio. Alex Wong | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Thursday defended a controversial ad by the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar. Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur.In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life.""Don't vote for people who lie," Arthur says in the ad. "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse."Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004.Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse.""The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him."The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday.Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing.""I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said.Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim.Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate.But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America.""The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts."Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets.Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad.Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do.""My mother is not well," Acton said.Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested."Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down."The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line. I hope the ad will be taken down and the final days of the campaign will focus on policy differences."— CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this article.

schema.headline: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism

title: Blackstone's Jon Gray says CoreWeave can 'find a way through' financing pressure
description: CoreWeave has been battered over concerns about its massive debt, but Blackstone chief operating officer Jon Gray believes the so-called neocloud comp
body: CoreWeave has been battered over concerns about its massive debt, but Blackstone chief operating officer Jon Gray believes the so-called neocloud company will weather the storm. Right now, CoreWeave and its neocloud peers are facing challenges over the capital needed to deliver on their promises, he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box" Thursday."Some of these companies have very talented CEOs. CoreWeave is a good example of this," Gray said. "They'll find a way through it, but that's the challenge they face. The underlying business is actually quite strong."CoreWeave has seen its stock sink, bond yields rise and spreads on its credit default swaps widen over the past week as investors became nervous about how the company will continue to finance its data centers, and at what cost. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreweave's one-month performanceDemand for computing power, however, is strong, said Gray. He is seeing that across the board in the private companies the firm holds. At the same time, there is a constraint in delivering supply, he said. "For the neo clouds, if they can get to the other side, the pricing of compute is up 50%," he said. "Their legacy chips are worth much more than people thought. Their data centers are leased below market."Shares of CoreWeave sank 3.55% on Thursday, and are down 14% over the past week. Blackstone earningsGray spoke with CNBC after Blackstone reported its third-quarter results, which came in mixed. Its stock was up 4% on Thursday. Blackstone saw quarterly revenue of $3.22 billion, short of the $3.28 billion expected from analysts polled by LSEG. Its adjusted earnings of $1.32 per share, however, topped the $1.26 consensus estimate. It was a "challenging quarter with markets" thanks to high energy prices and the rise in Treasury yields, Gray said. However, the firm delivered for its clients, he noted. "Across the board, our flagship strategies beat comparable public market indices and that's what we care most about," he said. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBlackstone year to dateHe anticipates a strong fourth quarter and 2027, despite some cross-currents like the rising cost of capital, government deficits and some crowding out of capital due to the AI infrastructure build. However, good news is there is underlying economic and earnings strength, he said. Gray also expects initial public offerings to resume once the market and geopolitical situation calms a bit. He said investors just need to have some patience."We have a long-term approach, and we feel very good about where we position capital for our investors, the growth of those companies, the growth of those assets, and that's what gives us confidence," he said. "At some point, the wider window will open, and when that happens, we and others will sell even more."

schema.headline: Blackstone's Jon Gray says CoreWeave can 'find a way through' financing pressure

title: Lawsuit accuses Trump of illegally profiting off foreign crypto deals
description: President Donald Trump speaks during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Oct. 21, 2026.Saul Loeb | AFP | Getty ImagesA law
body: President Donald Trump speaks during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Oct. 21, 2026.Saul Loeb | AFP | Getty ImagesA lawsuit filed Thursday accuses President Donald Trump and his family's crypto company of "corruptly profiting" off more than $2 billion in digital currency-related deals, violating constitutional restrictions on accepting foreign money."No president in American history has profited from his office so brazenly," alleges the federal civil complaint from a shareholder of Circle Internet Group, a publicly traded U.S. crypto company and competitor of the Trump family business, World Liberty Financial.The suit filed in U.S. District Court in Washington by shareholder and former Circle employee J. Benjamin Greenberg centers on two allegedly "illegal foreign emoluments" involving World Liberty and Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the national security advisor to the United Arab Emirates.Days before Trump's inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Tahnoon — widely known as the "Spy Sheikh" because of his powerful intelligence role — agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million. The company told The Wall Street Journal, which revealed the transaction in January 2026, that Trump had no involvement in the deal. But Trump would receive millions of dollars from that purchase after becoming president, according to his financial disclosures.The lawsuit also highlights a "scheme" by an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund chaired by Tahnoon to "inflate the value of President Trump's crypto holdings" through last year's purchase of $2 billion in World Liberty's stablecoin, USD1.The lawsuit asserts the conduct violates the U.S. Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause, which forbids federal officeholders from accepting money or other gifts from foreign officials without the consent of Congress."This sounds more like a partisan press release than a lawsuit," Bill Burck of Quinn Emanuel, counsel for World Liberty Financial, said in a statement. "All we know about it is from media reports. Anyone can file a lawsuit in America, even a frivolous one.""This is yet another frivolous lawsuit that echoes the same, tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family, and his administration for a decade," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CNBC in a statement. "There are no conflicts of interest."In a statement to CNBC, Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal representing Greenberg, said, "What President Trump did is brazenly corrupt. He's made millions from these deals by selling out the American people."We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," Pelikan said.The suit says Greenberg is filing derivatively on behalf of Circle. The company said in a statement to CNBC it was not behind the lawsuit and does not comment on pending litigation."Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing," the company said via a spokesperson.The suit names Trump, World Liberty and U.S. Middle East Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as defendants, as well as four related limited liability companies."World Liberty Financial is compliant with all U.S. laws and regulations," David Wachsman, a World Liberty spokesperson, told CNBC. "No one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government. These claims are without merit and we look forward to resolving them in court." The White House and a spokesperson for Witkoff did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the lawsuit.In addition to seeking a court declaration that Trump's profits violate the Constitution, Greenberg wants the president to disclose all other foreign crypto emoluments he's received and return any profits found to be illegal.Trump and his family have rapidly expanded their crypto business since he returned to the White House. World Liberty Financial, launched with members of the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024, operates the USD1 stablecoin, and an entity affiliated with Trump and his family owns about 38% of the company.The business has been highly lucrative for Trump even as investors in the so-called governance token WLFI suffered steep losses. Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto income in his 2025 annual financial disclosure, including nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty. WLFI, meanwhile, fell from about 45 cents in August 2025 to about 5 cents by the end of June 2026.The venture has drawn particular scrutiny over its ties to the UAE. Months after Tahnoon's 2025 investment, the administration expanded UAE access to advanced U.S. AI chips, including for G42, a UAE state-backed AI company controlled by Tahnoon.U.S. lawmakers have sought information about those dealings and signaled that Trump family business transactions could face further investigation if Democrats gain subpoena power in Congress in the 2026 midterm election.

schema.headline: Lawsuit accuses Trump of illegally profiting off foreign crypto deals

title: Brent crude tops $113, highest level since May, after Trump hints at action on Iran
description: watch nowOil prices spiked Thursday as investors fear escalation in the Middle East with the U.S. reportedly planning to resume strikes against Iran.B
body: watch nowOil prices spiked Thursday as investors fear escalation in the Middle East with the U.S. reportedly planning to resume strikes against Iran.Brent crude futures gained 4% to close at $113.17 per barrel, the highest level for the international benchmark since May 4. U.S. West Texas Intermediate gained 2.4% to settle at $99.47.  The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, unnamed U.S. officials told The New York Times. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, the officials said.President Donald Trump subsequently said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran when asked by a reporter late Wednesday. Trump said "something one way or the other" will "happen fairly soon" on Iran without elaborating.  "Most people seem to think it's after the election," Trump said. "We're going to see what happens." The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, dismissing reports that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave.Pigott pointed to escalating attacks by Iran-allied Houthis on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as the reason for the order. At least two people were killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Saudi Arabia's east coast Wednesday, according to Saudi state media.Meanwhile, oil giant Saudi Aramco has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely, people familiar with the matter told Reuters Thursday. Aramco facilities have repeatedly come under attack by the Houthis.The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors."$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs."I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

title: Bill Ackman says 2027 will be an amazing year for stocks as wars, inflation ease
description: watch nowPershing Square CEO Bill Ackman said two geopolitical conflicts — the Ukraine-Russia and Iran wars — along with elevated inflation and intere
body: watch nowPershing Square CEO Bill Ackman said two geopolitical conflicts — the Ukraine-Russia and Iran wars — along with elevated inflation and interest rates are holding back an otherwise "booming market environment.""Once the overhang of the war is done — and it sounds like we're also potentially heading in the right direction with Russia-Ukraine — energy prices could come way down, and obviously that would be very good for inflation and markets," Ackman told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "We're going to have an amazing 2027."Ackman, who called the Iran conflict an "extremely well-executed war," believes that once there's peace in the Middle East, it will be great for the region and "ultimately great for the United States."Higher crude prices have pressured stocks all year, as traders fear elevated energy costs will drive up inflation and force the Federal Reserve to raise rates. U.S. oil is up 72% in 2026, while Brent crude has surged 83%.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconWTI in 2026Rising oil appears to have trickled down to consumer prices. Gasoline prices accounted for over half of the increase in the latest consumer price index report. Inflation has been stubborn, moving away from the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September.Higher prices put the Fed in a bind to keep interest rates elevated to tame inflation.Cheap NetflixAckman also discussed individual long-term stock opportunities on his radar.The hedge fund manager said he viewed Netflix's earnings favorably. The streaming stock dropped more than 5% on Wednesday after reporting lackluster advertising and revenue guidance. On Thursday, however, they bounced more than 3%.Ackman said that any concerns around Netflix's content library are overblown when considering the strength of its management team and its engagement with users. He added that the stock is currently trading at 18 times earnings, "one of the lowest valuations in history," and expected to post earnings growth in the mid to high teens for the foreseeable future. "Netflix is a high growth utility," he said.Meta undervaluedThe billionaire investor also has Meta Platforms as a core part of Pershing Square's portfolio. Shares of the Facebook and Instagram parent are down 6% Thursday despite the company reporting better-than-expected revenue in its third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday, while issuing strong guidance for the current period.The stock's drop didn't faze Ackman. "We're in a world in which you cannot look at the day one trading of a stock after earnings because of how levered market participants are and how short-term they are," he said."Meta is extremely well positioned in democratizing the use of agents," citing the company's success with its personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse.Meta has "proven that AI is helping them accelerate their business and this remains an incredibly undervalued stock and that's why we own it," Ackman noted.He unveiled his position on the tech giant in February. At the time, Ackman cited Meta's "long-term upside potential from AI represents a deeply discounted valuation for one of the world's greatest businesses," during an investor presentation. Ackman believes Meta's investments in compute infrastructure are necessary and could eventually generate attractive returns.Fannie and Freddie going up tenfold?Ackman also reiterated his bullish stance on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, of which he is large shareholder in."These stocks will go up tenfold. and that's you know, that's the most asymmetric investment I'm aware of in the stock market," he said. "These entities have fully rebuilt their capital. What's not, I think, well understood is Fannie and Freddie today have five times the capital they had historically."

schema.headline: Bill Ackman says 2027 will be an amazing year for stocks as wars, inflation ease

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says neocloud demand is 'off the charts' but capital is scarce
description: watch nowNvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neocloud firms is "off the charts," but scarce capital is holding back growth."If
body: watch nowNvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neocloud firms is "off the charts," but scarce capital is holding back growth."If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neo clouds is off the charts," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin on Thursday, adding that capabilities are "extraordinary.""What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," Huang said."The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved," he added.Power is a major constraint for the AI boom, particularly in Europe, where electricity prices are higher. Huang said that the allocation of energy — which is scarce in the region — to companies like Nebius and Mistral is crucial for their growth."You can bring investments into Europe, but you have to start with having your own infrastructure," Huang explained. "If the neoclouds in Europe are able to establish an infrastructure here, then you can build the AI ecosystem, the AI economy on top of them, and then the flywheel of the AI economy will start in Europe. It will terminate in Europe."He added: "Across all of Europe, you're going to need a lot more neoclouds." Neoclouds under pressureNeocloud stocks such as CoreWeave and Nebius have been selling off recently as concerns grow over how much companies are spending on the AI infrastructure buildout, with the return on investments set to take longer than expected. Investors are also wary of how much debt CoreWeave, one of the biggest neocloud players, is using to fund its data center buildout. Neocloud stocks were lower in premarket trading on Thursday, with Nebius down 3.6%, and CoreWeave 4% lower. Iren and Applied Digital also shed nearly 4%. Huang has been on a European media blitz this month as the chip giant looks to expand investments in the region's AI sector. The company has committed nearly $10 billion towards companies, universities, and research institutions. While visiting London last week, Nvidia announced a stake worth over $1 billion in five U.K. startups. The chip giant is also investing in various French startups. "We're trying to kickstart the AI economy in Europe," Huang told CNBC. "Europe has a tremendous amount of technology, tremendous amount of industrial know-how, incredible science and technology, and it's ready to engage and build the AI economy here."

schema.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says neocloud demand is 'off the charts' but capital is scarce

title: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case
description: Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, listens during a reconvened legislative session to vote on Gov. Abigail Spanberger's amendments to the Virginia budge
body: Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, listens during a reconvened legislative session to vote on Gov. Abigail Spanberger's amendments to the Virginia budget, Monday, June 29, 2026 at the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond, Va. (Mike Kropf/Richmond Times-Dispatch via Getty Images)Mike Kropf | Richmond Times-dispatch | Getty ImagesVirginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas has been charged in a federal indictment with leading an alleged marijuana racketeering conspiracy that included family members of the powerful Democrat, according to court documents made public on Thursday.The indictment and the FBI said the five-year scheme, which was worth an estimated $4.5 million, obtained and illegally distributed "large quantities of illegal marijuana," and aimed to procure "generational wealth" for members of the enterprise.Lucas, 82, is a critic of President Donald Trump, and was an architect of ultimately failed efforts in Virginia to redraw the state's congressional map for November to boost chances for Democrats to win certain districts. She also has been a proponent of legalizing marijuana in the state.The criminal case, which also charges members of Lucas' family, was made public by the Department of Justice less than two weeks before the midterm election. Those contests will determine what political party controls both chambers of Congress.Lucas, the state Senate's president pro tempore and chairman of the Finance and Appropriations Committee, is not on the ballot this year. The indictment alleges that Lucas, who was first elected to the Senate in 1991, leveraged her position as chairman of the powerful committee to protect her marijuana enterprise.The indictment says Lucas "was the leader of the enterprise," that she "arranged for the acquisition and distribution of marijuana, supervises the laundering of marijuana proceeds," and "used her political influence to attempt to influence Virginia legislation for the benefit of herself and her family and maintained a premise for the distribution of marijuana." The alleged scheme used two stores, CBD Shopped and The Cannabis Outlet, for its operation."On May 6, the FBI executed federal search warrants at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe," the Department of Justice said in a statement. "Agents recovered marijuana and firearms at both locations."Six other defendants are charged in the alleged scheme, among them Lucas' two daughters and her grandson, Ryan Eichelbeger. One of the daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke, is running for mayor of Portsmouth. Lucas is in custody with the other defendants, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced at a press conference Thursday. She is scheduled to appear before a magistrate judge in U.S. District Court in Norfolk, Virginia, at 2:30 p.m. ET Thursday.In addition to racketeering conspiracy, Lucas is charged with conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana; conspiracy to launder money; conspiracy to commit honest services fraud; and maintaining a drug involved premises."Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother," Lucas said in a statement posted on X."I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now," she said. "I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down."Blanche, when asked at the press conference about criticism from Lucas's attorney that the case is politically motivated, said, "We don't do political paybacks." The attorney general noted the investigation of Lucas began before the current Trump administration, and that a federal grand jury had determined there was enough evidence to indict her."There's decision and processes in place at the department when we're bringing a case against a political official, and the ... first question is: is this investigation proper?" Blanche said. "And the conclusion of that is yes. Is the timing proper? And the conclusion of that is yes."The indictment was issued by a grand jury on Oct. 14, but was only unsealed Thursday.Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, in a statement, said,"In our American system of justice, people are presumed innocent until proven guilty, and that is true for Senator L. Louise Lucas.""She and her family deserve the opportunity to present their defense and speak to the allegations presented," Spanberger said.The governor also said, "The timing of this indictment undermines the U.S. Department of Justice's previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions — to include indictments or significant investigative steps — close to an election and sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice."The indictment says that after he was hired in 2022, a senior law enforcement officer "warned Louise Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and was going to get her in trouble one day."Lucas since 2021 has been a partner in The Cannabis Outlet, a shop that sells selling hemp and CBD, or cannabidiol products. After a 2024 burglary at the store, two of Lucas' co-defendants claimed to Portsmouth Police that about $3,000 of marijuana products were missing.One of the overt acts listed in the indictment was an April 2022 meeting between Lucas, her two daughters and an indicted co-conspirator at Lucas' office. At that meeting, the indictment alleges, Lucas asked the unidentified co-conspirator "if they were a member of law enforcement before purchasing between three and five pounds of marijuana" from the co-conspirator with a check for $6,600 from Lisa Lucas-Burke. The check was made out to "Freedom is Dope."On Feb. 5, 2026, the indictment says, Lucas called an unindicted co-conspirator and discussed the language surrounding the recreational marijuana legislation pending in the Virginia General Assembly, and the possibility of [the co-conspirator] receiving a license and sharing the proceeds with her because 'this is our last chance at generational wealth . . .. I've got too old to not be greedy.'"The charges come five months after FBI agents executed a search warrant at Lucas' Portsmouth office.At the time of that May 6 raid, Lucas noted in a statement that it came two weeks after Virginia voters approved the redistricting plan, adding, "Virginians sent a powerful message when they voted to stop Trump's scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections.""I was proud to help lead that effort and I have never been afraid to stand up to Donald Trump."

schema.headline: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case
